summary: Discusses how to extend the DNS with new data for a new application. It lists different mechanisms and concludes that a new resource record type is the best solution, rather than overloading the TXT record, which discussions too often favor.

plainLanguage.summary: If you want to store a new kind of information, you can stuff it into a general box or make a new labeled box. This note says making a new labeled box is usually the better idea.

subtitle: Why a new resource record type is the best way to add data to the DNS.

tldr.problem: When applications need to store new kinds of data in the DNS, designers often choose to reuse the TXT record type because it accepts any text. However, TXT records lack defined structure, create collision risks, can cause messages to exceed packet size limits, and complicate DNSSEC signing.
tldr.mechanism: The document evaluates five extension mechanisms: selectors inside existing record data, prefixes in domain names, suffixes in domain names, new DNS classes, and new resource record types. It explains the trade-offs of each approach.
tldr.outcome: Despite historical difficulties with new record types, modern DNS infrastructure now handles them well. Creating a new resource record type is cleaner than reusing TXT records and avoids most of the problems associated with alternative extension mechanisms.

facts.label: Maximum DNS message size over UDP

today: RFC 5507 is Informational and provides guidance for DNS extension design. It has not been obsoleted. Modern DNS deployments follow its recommendation to use new resource record types rather than overloading TXT records.

sections.title: The DNS Extension Problem
sections.content:
The DNS stores many categories of data: infrastructure records (NS, SOA), address mappings (A, AAAA, PTR), mail routing (MX), and application-specific records (SRV, NAPTR). When designing a new application, developers must decide how to store its data in the DNS while minimizing impact on existing applications and keeping DNS messages small enough to fit in UDP packets.

A DNS query consists of three parts: an owner (or name), a resource record class, and a resource record type. The challenge is to ensure precise selection of what data to return so that applications get only what they need. Historically, different applications have extended the DNS in different ways (MX as a new type, SRV using prefixes, NAPTR using subtyping), leading to inconsistent approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: The DNS needs to store all kinds of information for different applications. When you invent a new application, you have to decide how to add its data to the DNS without breaking the existing system.

sections.title: Five Extension Mechanisms and Their Trade-Offs
sections.content:
Selectors inside RDATA (subtyping): Multiple applications share one record type and distinguish their data using selectors inside the record data (as in NAPTR and the old KEY record). The disadvantage is that a client must fetch the entire RRSet and parse it to find the relevant records. This increases message size and risk of UDP packet overflow, forcing fallback to TCP, which increases server load.

Prefix in domain name: Add an application-specific prefix to the domain name (as in SRV records with '_service._proto'). This allows separate RRSets for each application but has problems with DNS wildcards, which only work when '*' is the leftmost label. Prefixes also require separate zone management if the data belongs in a different zone from related data.

Suffix in domain name: Create a parallel tree with a suffix (e.g., 'example.com' and 'example.com._bar'). This minimizes RRSet size but creates synchronization and update authorization issues since data for a single entity is split across two different zones administered separately.

New DNS class: In theory, new classes (like HS for Hesiod) could distinguish data types, but this is impractical. Classes are tied to the delegation tree, so changing classes may cross administrative boundaries unpredictably. Only the IN class has ever seen widespread deployment.

New resource record type: Create a new record type designed specifically for the application's data. This was historically difficult due to infrastructure limitations, but modern DNS now handles unknown record types well (per RFC 3597). It cleanly separates different applications' data into distinct RRSets.
sections.plainLanguage: You can add data by (1) mixing it with other data in the same box and using labels to sort it, (2) changing the name to put it in a different box, (3) using a different naming branch, (4) creating a whole different filing system, or (5) just making a new labeled box. Each approach has problems except the last one.

sections.title: Why TXT Records Are Problematic
sections.content:
The TXT record appears attractive because it accepts arbitrary text with no predefined structure. However, this flexibility creates serious problems. First, TXT records lack semantic collision prevention: applications create their own syntax and structure within TXT records, making it impossible to reliably distinguish one application's records from another's. A parser encountering unexpected TXT record data may misinterpret it.

Second, TXT records create size problems. Verbose text encodings of application data are inefficient compared to binary formats. When an entire RRSet must be returned together (as required by DNS caching), size can grow rapidly, increasing the risk of UDP packet overflow and forcing TCP fallback. This substantially increases load on servers since TCP requires the server to maintain connection state.

Third, combinations of TXT records with naming modifications (prefixes or suffixes) still lack a standardized subtype field, making collisions likely. Any attempt to impose standardization now is too late given decades of existing TXT record uses.
sections.plainLanguage: TXT records are like blank paper: you can write anything, but then two people might write incompatible things on different papers and cause confusion. Plus, if you stuff too much data in TXT records, the DNS message gets too big to send.

sections.title: Benefits of a New Resource Record Type
sections.content:
A new resource record type provides several advantages. It creates clear semantics: the type definition specifies exactly what the data means and how it is structured, eliminating collision risk. Clients can query for exactly what they want, getting a precise RRSet without unwanted data.

It enables compact binary representation tailored to the application's needs, reducing message size and the risk of UDP overflow. It allows DNSSEC signing to operate cleanly on the specific RRSet rather than signing a large mixed set of data from multiple applications.

The historical concern that adding new record types is difficult has been addressed. Modern investigations show that deployed DNS software widely supports RFC 3597 (generic handling of unknown record types). The approval process for new types has also improved (RFC 5395), making the effort more predictable. While provisioning tools may require updates to support new record types, this is a minor difference compared to the problems with alternative approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: A new record type is like creating a labeled box just for one kind of document. The label prevents confusion, you can pack things efficiently, and everyone knows what goes where.

sections.title: Recommendation
sections.content: While there is no magic solution for painlessly adding data to the DNS, the document concludes that creating a new resource record type, following RFC 5395, is the preferred approach in most cases. The most obvious approach of using TXT records for arbitrary application data is almost certainly the worst option, particularly because of the problems with lack of semantics and message size. Protocol designers should not be deterred by historical difficulties but should use the resource record type mechanism designed precisely for this purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: When you need to store new data in the DNS, make a new record type. It is the cleanest solution and the infrastructure now supports it.
